title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening cerebrovascular disorder caused by thrombosis of the dural venous sinuses, cerebral veins, or both, resulting in impaired venous drainage and elevated intracranial pressure. This course outlines the clinical presentation of CVST, which varies widely, ranging from isolated headache to focal neurologic deficits, seizures, or coma, often mimicking other neurologic emergencies, and its underlying pathophysiology, which reflects venous outflow obstruction and parenchymal injury driven by venous congestion, ischemia, and hemorrhagic transformation. Risk factors that are frequently multifactorial and align with Virchow’s triad, including inherited thrombophilias such as factor V Leiden mutation, systemic inflammatory disease, malignancy, pregnancy, infection, medications, trauma, and iatrogenic causes, are also discussed.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity reviews the appropriate imaging and laboratory evaluation of CVST as well as the interpretation of diagnostic findings. Participants will also gain an understanding of evidence-based management, including anticoagulation strategies, approaches to intracranial hypertension, seizure management, and indications for endovascular or surgical intervention. Special scenarios such as pregnancy, septic CVST, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia are addressed. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying CSVT, performing the recommended evaluation, applying risk stratification, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition to optimize patient outcomes and safety.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Introduction
content: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) refers to the formation of a blood clot within the dural venous sinuses, cerebral veins, or both, leading to impaired cerebral venous drainage and elevated intracranial pressure. CVST is a rare but serious condition with variable clinical presentations that can mimic other neurologic emergencies. The signs and symptoms depend on the location and extent of venous occlusion. Commonly affected sites include the superior sagittal sinus and the lateral sinuses (transverse and sigmoid) and, less frequently, the cavernous sinus and deep cerebral venous system. Cortical vein thrombosis is less common and often occurs with associated sinus thrombosis. Early recognition and appropriate management are essential to reduce morbidity and mortality. (see Image . Cerebral Venous Sinus System)

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Etiology
content: CVST results from conditions that promote venous stasis, endothelial injury, or hypercoagulability, consistent with Virchow’s triad. [1] The etiology is frequently multifactorial, and affected patients often have more than 1 contributing risk factor. These factors may be broadly classified as permanent or transient, although overlap may occur.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Etiology -- Permanent Risk Factors
content: Inherited and acquired thrombophilias are among the most common permanent risk factors and include prothrombin G20210A mutation, factor V Leiden mutation, protein C deficiency, protein S deficiency, antithrombin deficiency, and antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Etiology -- Permanent Risk Factors
content: Hematologic disorders associated with chronic hypercoagulability include paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, sickle cell disease or trait, and myeloproliferative neoplasms, eg, polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Etiology -- Permanent Risk Factors
content: Autoimmune, vasculitic, and systemic inflammatory conditions contribute to endothelial dysfunction and thrombosis risk. These include Behçet disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren syndrome, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, inflammatory bowel disease, sarcoidosis, nephrotic syndrome, and thyroid disorders.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Etiology -- Permanent Risk Factors
content: Malignancy is a well-established risk factor and may involve primary central nervous system tumors, solid tumors outside the central nervous system, or hematologic malignancies, eg, leukemia and lymphoma.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Etiology -- Transient Risk Factors
content: Hormonal and reproductive factors play a prominent role, particularly in younger patients, and include oral contraceptive use, pregnancy, the postpartum period, and hormone replacement therapy.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Etiology -- Transient Risk Factors
content: Infections may precipitate CVST through local extension or systemic inflammation. These include intracranial infections; infections of the ear, sinuses, face, mouth, and neck; and systemic infections, eg, sepsis, endocarditis, tuberculosis, and human immunodeficiency virus infection.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Etiology -- Transient Risk Factors
content: Metabolic and systemic stressors associated with transient hypercoagulability include severe dehydration, severe anemia, and diabetic ketoacidosis.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Etiology -- Transient Risk Factors
content: Medications implicated in CVST include glucocorticoids, androgen therapy, selected chemotherapeutic agents (eg, L-asparaginase and cyclosporine), selective estrogen receptor modulators (including tamoxifen), angiogenesis inhibitors (such as thalidomide), and hemostatic agents.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Epidemiology
content: Recent population-based studies suggest that the incidence of CVST is higher than previously recognized. Contemporary estimates from high-income countries indicate an annual incidence of approximately 1 to 2 cases per 100,000 adults. [3] [4] This apparent increase over time is likely multifactorial, reflecting improved disease recognition with widespread availability of advanced neuroimaging, as well as potential changes in the prevalence of predisposing risk factors. [5]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Epidemiology
content: In the United States, CVST accounts for less than 1% of all stroke admissions, though its relative contribution has increased over the past 2 decades. Population-based analyses have demonstrated a rising proportion of stroke hospitalizations attributable to CVST, with notable increases among men and older women. Epidemiologic data from low- and middle-income countries remain limited, highlighting an important gap in global CVST research. [6]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Epidemiology
content: CVST disproportionately affects women of reproductive age, with incidence rates around 3-fold higher than those observed in age-matched men. [7] [8] This sex difference is largely attributed to hormonal and pregnancy-related risk factors, including oral contraceptive use, pregnancy, and the postpartum period. Emerging data also suggest possible racial differences in CVST incidence, with some studies indicating higher rates among Black individuals in the United States, though the underlying causes and generalizability of these findings require further investigation. [9]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Pathophysiology
content: CVST results from obstruction of cerebral venous outflow, leading to a cascade of hemodynamic and cellular changes that ultimately cause neurological dysfunction. The pathophysiology involves 2 primary mechanisms: impaired venous drainage, leading to elevated intracranial pressure, and localized venous congestion, resulting in parenchymal injury. [10]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Pathophysiology
content: Venous outflow obstruction leads to increased venous and capillary pressure within the affected drainage territory. This rise in pressure reduces cerebrospinal fluid absorption at the arachnoid granulations, contributing to intracranial hypertension, which commonly manifests as headache, papilledema, and visual disturbances.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Pathophysiology
content: Venous congestion and reduced cerebral perfusion pressure impair oxygen delivery and disrupt the blood–brain barrier. This process promotes vasogenic edema, which may progress to cytotoxic edema as ischemia worsens. Unlike arterial stroke, venous infarction often crosses arterial territories and is frequently associated with hemorrhagic transformation due to rupture of congested venules and capillaries.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Pathophysiology
content: Involvement of cortical veins or the deep venous system can result in focal neurological deficits, seizures, altered mental status, or coma. Thrombosis of the deep cerebral veins and straight sinus is particularly associated with bilateral thalamic involvement and a more severe clinical course. The inflammatory response to thrombosis further exacerbates endothelial dysfunction and promotes thrombus propagation. In some cases, collateral venous channels partially compensate for impaired drainage, which may explain the wide variability in clinical presentation and disease severity. [11] [12]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- History and Physical -- Clinical History
content: The clinical presentation of CVST is highly variable and often nonspecific, which may delay diagnosis. Symptoms may develop acutely, subacutely, or chronically and are influenced by the location and extent of venous involvement, as well as the presence of intracranial hypertension or parenchymal injury.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- History and Physical -- Clinical History
content: Headache is the most common presenting symptom and may be diffuse or localized, progressive, or sudden in onset. CVST is frequently associated with features of increased intracranial pressure, including nausea, vomiting, and visual disturbances. Focal neurologic deficits may develop hours to days after headache onset and occur in approximately half of patients. These deficits are often related to venous infarction or hemorrhage and may include motor weakness, sensory deficits, aphasia, or visual field abnormalities. Leg weakness or hemiparesis may result from infarction in the frontoparietal regions draining into the vein of Trolard, while aphasia and confusion may occur due to involvement of the temporal lobe drainage territory of the vein of Labbé. Sigmoid sinus thrombosis can present with mastoid pain and, rarely, lower cranial nerve palsies.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- History and Physical -- Clinical History
content: Seizures are more common in CVST than in arterial stroke and may be focal or generalized. Altered mental status, ranging from confusion to coma, is more frequently observed in patients with extensive sinus involvement or deep cerebral venous thrombosis and is often associated with elevated intracranial pressure. Cranial nerve palsies, particularly involving cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, may suggest cavernous sinus involvement.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: On physical examination, findings may include papilledema, focal neurologic deficits, or signs of systemic infection, malignancy, or inflammatory disease. Fever may be present in infection-associated cases. Examination of the head and neck may reveal evidence of sinusitis, otitis, or mastoiditis in appropriate clinical contexts. A careful history should assess for risk factors, including recent pregnancy or postpartum status, oral contraceptive use, hormone replacement therapy, malignancy, infection, dehydration, recent trauma or procedures, and known thrombophilia. [13]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Imaging
content: The diagnosis of CVST requires a high index of suspicion due to its variable and often nonspecific clinical presentation. [14] Clinical features, associated risk factors, and neuroimaging findings guide evaluation.
contents: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Imaging. The diagnosis of CVST requires a high index of suspicion due to its variable and often nonspecific clinical presentation. [14] Clinical features, associated risk factors, and neuroimaging findings guide evaluation.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Imaging
content: Noncontrast computed tomography (CT) of the head is frequently the initial imaging study obtained in patients with suspected CVST. CT findings may include direct visualization of a hyperdense thrombosed sinus in the acute phase, which can evolve to isodense and later hypodense appearances over time. [15] Indirect findings include venous infarction, intracerebral hemorrhage, cerebral edema, or mass effect. Characteristic signs, such as the dense triangle sign in superior sagittal sinus thrombosis and the cord sign in cortical venous thrombosis, may be present. [16] Juxtacortical hemorrhages that are small, concave in shape, and located within the subcortical white matter have also been described. [17] However, noncontrast CT may be normal in a substantial proportion of patients and does not exclude the diagnosis.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Imaging
content: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides greater sensitivity for detecting venous thrombosis across disease stages. MRI provides improved visualization of thrombus evolution  and associated parenchymal abnormalities, including venous infarction, hemorrhage, vasogenic edema, and sulcal effacement. Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI may demonstrate the empty delta sign, reflecting central nonopacification of a thrombosed superior sagittal sinus surrounded by peripheral enhancement. [18]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Imaging
content: CT venography (CTV) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) are the preferred tests to confirm CVST when clinical suspicion is present. These studies directly demonstrate venous sinus occlusion or filling defects. CTV offers rapid acquisition and wide availability, whereas MRV provides superior soft tissue resolution and avoids ionizing radiation. MRV may be performed using noncontrast techniques, most commonly time-of-flight (TOF) or phase-contrast imaging, or with contrast-enhanced methods. TOF MRV remains widely used and is particularly useful when contrast is undesirable or cannot be given (for example, in severe renal impairment). In pregnancy, gadolinium is generally avoided unless essential; breastfeeding does not usually require interruption after gadolinium administration, but mothers may choose to abstain for 12 to 24 hours if concerned. [19] In cases where absent venous flow may represent congenital hypoplasia rather than thrombosis, evaluation of associated bony anatomy on CT may aid differentiation. [20]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Evaluation -- Diagnostic Imaging
content: When noninvasive venographic studies are inconclusive and clinical suspicion remains high, digital subtraction angiography may be considered, though this modality is rarely required due to advances in noninvasive imaging. Delayed or absent opacification of cerebral veins or dural sinuses on angiography supports the diagnosis of acute venous thrombosis. [15]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Studies
content: Laboratory evaluation should be guided by the clinical context and include basic studies such as complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function tests, and coagulation parameters. Testing for inherited or acquired thrombophilia may be considered, particularly in younger patients or those without an identifiable provoking factor. However, such testing is often deferred until the acute phase has resolved. D-dimer testing may be elevated in acute CVST but lacks sufficient sensitivity to exclude the diagnosis and should not be used as a standalone screening test. [21] Lumbar puncture is generally reserved for cases in which central nervous system infection is suspected, and meningitis needs to be excluded. [1]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management
content: The primary goals of treatment in CVST are to prevent thrombus propagation, promote recanalization, manage intracranial hypertension, and treat underlying causes or complications.
contents: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management. The primary goals of treatment in CVST are to prevent thrombus propagation, promote recanalization, manage intracranial hypertension, and treat underlying causes or complications.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Anticoagulation
content: Anticoagulation is the cornerstone of treatment for CVST and should be initiated promptly in all patients without contraindications, including those with venous hemorrhage related to venous infarction. Current American Heart Association/American Stroke Association and European guidance recommends initial therapy with therapeutic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) or unfractionated heparin (UFH), followed by transition to oral anticoagulation. LMWH is generally preferred in the acute setting due to its ease of administration, more predictable anticoagulant effects, and lower risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, with observational data suggesting improved outcomes. Unfractionated heparin may be favored in patients with renal impairment or when rapid reversal is required. [19] [22]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Anticoagulation
content: Following the acute phase, patients are transitioned to oral anticoagulation, traditionally with vitamin K antagonists. The underlying risk profile guides treatment duration and typically ranges from 3 to 12 months for transient provoking factors, while long-term or indefinite therapy may be considered in the presence of persistent major risk factors or recurrent venous thromboembolism. [1] The role of venous sinus recanalization in determining anticoagulation duration remains uncertain. [23]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Anticoagulation
content: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) have emerged as alternative options to vitamin K antagonists in selected patients. [24] [25] [26] Available evidence from randomized and observational studies suggests comparable rates of recurrent venous thromboembolism, major bleeding, and venous recanalization. Based on current data, transition to either a DOAC or a vitamin K antagonist after an initial period of parenteral anticoagulation is reasonable. However, the optimal duration of this lead-in phase remains unclear. DOACs should be avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and caution is warranted in high-risk antiphospholipid syndrome or other situations where DOACs are not recommended.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Supportive Care
content: Management of intracranial hypertension is critical and includes head elevation, analgesia, and treatment of nausea and vomiting. In patients with severe or refractory intracranial pressure elevation, additional measures such as osmotic therapy may be required. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation is recommended in patients with papilledema to monitor visual function. [1]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Supportive Care
content: Seizures are treated with antiepileptic medications when clinically indicated. Routine prophylactic antiepileptic therapy is not recommended in the absence of seizures; it may be considered on a case-by-case basis in patients at high risk (for example, those with supratentorial hemorrhagic/infarct lesions). [27]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Endovascular therapy
content: Endovascular therapy (EVT) has been explored as a means to achieve more rapid venous recanalization in cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; however, its impact on clinical outcomes remains uncertain. [1] [28] Randomized and observational studies have not demonstrated a clear benefit of EVT over standard anticoagulation in unselected patients. [29] [30] The TO-ACT randomized clinical trial showed no improvement in functional outcomes among patients with severe CVST treated with EVT compared with anticoagulation alone. [31] Observational comparisons are limited by strong confounding by indication, and meta-analytic findings are inconsistent; overall, there is no proven outcome benefit of EVT over anticoagulation in unselected patients. [32] [33] [34]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Endovascular therapy
content: At present, EVT is generally reserved as a rescue therapy for carefully selected patients who experience clinical deterioration despite adequate anticoagulation or who have contraindications to standard medical therapy. [30] Various techniques have been described, including mechanical thrombectomy, catheter-directed thrombolysis, and combined approaches; however, no single method is superior. While high rates of venous recanalization have been reported in selected series, EVT is associated with a measurable risk of complications, and patient selection remains critical. [19]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical intervention
content: Surgical intervention, eg, decompressive hemicraniectomy, may be lifesaving in patients with malignant cerebral edema, impending herniation, or refractory intracranial hypertension. [35] Observational studies and systematic reviews suggest that early surgical intervention, particularly when performed within the first 48 hours of hospitalization, may reduce mortality and improve functional outcomes in selected patients with severe cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. [36] Identification and treatment of underlying etiologies, including infection, malignancy, or systemic inflammatory disease, are essential components of comprehensive management.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Pregnancy and postpartum management
content: In pregnancy, low-molecular-weight heparin is the preferred anticoagulant for acute CVST and is continued throughout pregnancy, with postpartum anticoagulation continued for at least 6 weeks and for a minimum total treatment duration consistent with other CVST cases. Vitamin K antagonists may be used postpartum if appropriate, and direct oral anticoagulants should be avoided during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Future pregnancy is not contraindicated; patients with prior CVST should receive individualized counselling, and prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin is often considered in subsequent pregnancies, particularly if the index event was pregnancy-related or if persistent risk factors are present.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia-associated CVT (postvaccination CVT with thrombocytopenia)
content: A rare but important special scenario is cerebral venous thrombosis associated with vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT) following adenoviral vector COVID-19 vaccination. Suspect VITT in patients presenting 5–30 days after vaccination with CVST plus thrombocytopenia and markedly elevated D-dimer. Management differs from typical CVST: avoid heparin and platelet transfusion (unless life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery), send PF4 antibody testing, initiate a non-heparin anticoagulant, and administer intravenous immunoglobulin.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Septic CVST
content: Septic CVST is an important special scenario in which thrombosis arises from adjacent or systemic infection (for example, mastoiditis/otitis media, sinusitis, facial or dental infections, meningitis, or sepsis). It should be suspected when CVST presents with fever, systemic toxicity, meningeal signs, or a clear head-and-neck infectious source. Management requires prompt intravenous antibiotics and urgent source control (ENT, dental, or neurosurgical input, as appropriate) in addition to CVST-directed therapy; anticoagulation is often still used but should be individualized based on intracranial hemorrhage, procedural needs, and overall bleeding risk.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- Cavernous sinus thrombosis
content: Cavernous sinus thrombosis is often infection-related and is typically discussed separately because it presents with prominent orbital features (periorbital edema, chemosis, proptosis), painful ophthalmoplegia, and cranial nerve III/IV/VI palsies with possible V1/V2 sensory involvement; cavernous sinus thrombosis is a medical emergency requiring immediate broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, rapid evaluation for the infective focus, and contrast-enhanced imaging/venography to confirm the diagnosis, with anticoagulation considered on a case-by-case basis alongside the treating teams.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Treatment / Management -- CVST with hemorrhagic transformation
content: Start therapeutic anticoagulation (LMWH preferred; UFH if rapid reversal may be needed or renal impairment is present), plus standard neurocritical care (ICP management, seizure control). Early neurosurgical consultation is indicated for patients with decreasing consciousness, significant midline shift or mass effect, large hemorrhagic venous infarct, or refractory intracranial hypertension. Decompressive hemicraniectomy may be considered in these settings, particularly when there is clinical or imaging evidence of brain herniation or raised intracranial pressure, although the evidence base is less robust than for arterial stroke or traumatic brain injury.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Arterial ischemic stroke : Typically follows defined arterial territories and lacks venous congestion on imaging. Intracerebral hemorrhage : May result from hypertension, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, vascular malformations, or hemorrhagic tumors, usually without associated venous sinus occlusion. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension : Presents with headache and papilledema, may include sixth nerve palsy. Venous imaging shows no thrombosis, though transverse sinus stenosis is common. Central nervous system infection : Meningitis or encephalitis should be considered in patients with fever, altered mental status, or meningeal signs. Intracranial neoplasm : Primary or metastatic tumors may cause headache, seizures, or focal deficits and typically show mass lesions on imaging. Subarachnoid hemorrhage : May present with acute headache and neurologic symptoms and should be excluded with appropriate imaging.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of CVST has improved substantially with early recognition and appropriate treatment. Most patients experience favorable functional outcomes, particularly when diagnosis and anticoagulation are initiated promptly.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Prognosis
content: Mortality rates are relatively low compared with arterial stroke but increase in the presence of coma at presentation, deep cerebral venous system involvement, intracerebral hemorrhage, underlying malignancy, or central nervous system infection. Recanalization of the affected venous sinuses occurs in many patients over time, although clinical recovery does not always correlate with the degree of radiographic recanalization.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Prognosis
content: Long-term neurological sequelae may include persistent headache, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, or visual impairment, especially in patients with delayed diagnosis or severe initial presentation. Recurrent CVST is uncommon but may occur, particularly in patients with ongoing prothrombotic risk factors. [37]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Complications
content: Potential complications of CVST include headache, visual loss (optic neuropathy due to papilledema), venous infarction (often hemorrhagic), seizures, intracerebral hemorrhage, and, less commonly, subarachnoid or subdural hemorrhage.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: In patients with recurrent CVST/VTE or persistent major prothrombotic risk factors, extended or indefinite anticoagulation may be considered. For many inherited thrombophilias, duration should be individualized rather than automatic. Patients need to be educated on the importance and rationale of continued anticoagulation. The decision to anticoagulate should be made in consultation with the patient, taking into account their predisposing thrombophilia and the risk it poses. Antiphospholipid syndrome, particularly with a persistent high-risk aPL profile, carries a higher risk of recurrent thrombosis and often warrants long-term anticoagulation. [38]

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: CVST is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening cerebrovascular disorder caused by thrombosis of the dural venous sinuses or cerebral veins, resulting in impaired venous drainage, elevated intracranial pressure, and possible venous infarction or hemorrhage. Clinical presentation is highly variable, ranging from isolated headache to focal neurologic deficits, seizures, or coma, which often delays diagnosis. Risk factors are frequently multifactorial and include inherited thrombophilias, malignancy, infection, pregnancy, medications, trauma, and systemic inflammatory disease. Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion and confirmation with CT or MR venography. Prompt anticoagulation remains the cornerstone of therapy, even in the presence of hemorrhagic venous infarction, with additional management directed at intracranial hypertension, seizures, and underlying causes.

title: Venous Sinus Thrombosis -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimizing outcomes requires coordinated interprofessional care. Physicians, general practitioners, and advanced practitioners must rapidly recognize red flags, initiate evidence-based anticoagulation, and determine the need for neurology, neurosurgery, or critical care consultation. Nurses play a central role in neurologic monitoring, seizure precautions, intracranial pressure management, and patient education. Pharmacists ensure safe anticoagulant selection, dosing, monitoring, and transition of therapy, particularly in pregnancy or renal impairment. Effective communication among emergency, neurology, radiology, pharmacy, obstetrics, infectious disease, and critical care teams supports timely imaging, individualized risk assessment, and complication management. Clear care coordination, shared decision-making, and structured follow-up enhance patient safety, adherence, and long-term functional recovery.
